items.title: 68357_Jimmy Maxwell oral history interview
items.q: But by that time I had gone on to the Perry Como Show so I didn't care.

ctx.x: was when the orchestra would play for time that had not been sold commercially. The union gave them a special weekly price which was lower than commercial scale. But on the other hand, a station could not put on any commercial programs. If one of their what they called pilot programs, if they got sold to a sponsor, then the staff musicians wouldn't do it and they had to hire outside musicians and pay them a higher scale. Of course, the staff musicians could be hired but they would still have to be paid outside…

But little by little they sort of pushed the agencies out of that field and took it over themselves. So I think that by 1958, I think, when I was on the Como show, National Broadcasting Company then paid the musicians instead of Perry Como, and Perry Como paid the National Broadcasting Company a lump sum for the time and everything else. They furnished the musicians, the camera crew and so forth. So that used to be in the hands of the stars, all the networks did was just sell them time. They weren't involved in…
